forms: ancient author of the Apocalypse of the Secret Spirit of Nature
E0064.summary: An unnamed ancient author of the Apocalypse of the Secret Spirit of Nature, cited through Khunrath on the divine water.
E0064.body: Khunrath cites this author of the *Apocalypse of the Secret Spirit of Nature* on the divine water [I.1 ¶20]. The text gives nothing further about the author.

E0065.summary: Atwood's name for the experiment of nature that the Inquiry sets out to recover in its causal light.
E0065.body: Atwood states the aim of her Inquiry as an attempt to “recover the Ancient Experiment of nature into her Causal Light” [III.4 ¶2]. The record does not define the term any further. The context suggests it names the practical work the book reconstructs, but the text does not say so here.

E0066.summary: A group voice that, Atwood says, agrees with the metaphysician by proving the Universal Identity of Nature through experiment.
E0066.body: Atwood says the ancient physiologists and alchemists agree with the metaphysician because they prove the Universal Identity of Nature by experiment [II.4 ¶16]. She cites them as support.

E0067.summary: A group voice cited as having condemned both inner and material idolatry.
E0067.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860, a later layer), the ancient prophets are cited as having condemned both inner and material idolatry [APP ¶100].

E0068.summary: A group voice whose meaning of metempsychosis Atwood sets against the common, mistaken meaning.
E0068.body: Atwood contrasts the meaning the Ancient Schools of Divinity gave to metempsychosis with the common one, which she treats as mistaken [IV.2 ¶18]. She sides with the ancient schools.

E0069.summary: Atwood's most frequent group authority, cited throughout as support for the reality, experimental basis and discipline of the Hermetic wisdom and the Mysteries.
E0069.body:
Atwood cites “the ancients” almost always as support for her own positions:

- **Reality and experience.** They assert higher realities known through both intellect and experiment [I.2 ¶49]. For them the truth is the same experience in everyone, “one and the same in all, where difference is merged in objective union” [II.2 ¶13]. They held that the worst evil is not seeing one's own evil, and they gave warnings about how the Spirit is to be handled [II.2 ¶14].
- **Preparing the mind.** They warn against passive dreaming in the phantasy. Before contemplation, they require the mind to be cleared and made passive [II.2 ¶22]. They insisted on ways of removing the barriers to the Divine Light. Their Wisdom was gained by discipline, and it goes beyond reason without contradicting it [IV.4 ¶15, IV.4 ¶17].
- **Life and Being.** They held this life to be a lessening of existence [III.2 ¶50]. The “wise ancients” compared a state of Being that verges on annihilation to darkness for the eye [III.2 ¶54].
- **Figures of the union.** Atwood reads the pairs Peleus and Thetis, Earth and Heaven, Bacchus and Ariadne, and Jason and Medea as their prefigurations of the union of Mind and Universe: “This is the marriage, by the ancients so many times prefigured” [III.3 ¶15].
- **The Mysteries.** They are her authority for treating the Mysteries as real inductions. They found their whole philosophy in the vital experiment, and she weighs their philosophy against Physical science [IV.4 ¶5, IV.4 ¶9, IV.4 ¶13].

E0070.summary: A name in the book's list of authors, given with the work Opera Omnia Medica.
E0070.body: Libavius appears in a list of authors, and footnote n85 gives his *Opera Omnia Medica* [I.1 ¶70, I.1 n85]. The note calls it “A ponderous compilation.” [I.1 n85]. The record says nothing more about how Atwood uses him.

E0071.summary: In a quoted adept's words, the subtle spirit conceived when the quintessential nature is opened. It holds the divine act and is a direct beam of Wisdom from God.
E0071.body: This is the language of a quoted adept, not Atwood's own words. When the quintessential nature is opened, what is conceived is “the subtle altereity of the angelical spirit in which is the divine act, and immediate beam or Wisdom from God” [II.3 ¶52]. The record gives no plainer meaning.

E0072.summary: A treatise cited in a footnote as the source of the Latin sequence of illumination in a philosopher's passage.
E0072.body: Footnote n27 cites *Anima Magia Abscond.*, p. 27, as the source of the Latin sequence of illumination in the philosopher's passage, which includes “Eritque in te cum Lumine, Ignis” [IV.2 ¶41, IV.2 n27]. (Our translation: And there shall be in you, with the Light, Fire.)

E0073.summary: Atwood's term for the middle soul or center of man or of nature, which she identifies with the medial center.
E0073.body: This entry comes from the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860, a later layer). There Atwood speaks of “the medial center, the anima media”: the middle soul or center of man or of nature [APP ¶147]. According to the record, this center can only be obtained together with its law, which is an impulse toward rectification and regeneration. **Identity:** = medial center [APP ¶147].

E0074.summary: The Ethnics' doctrine of the Anima Mundi, which Atwood says differs from Hebrew doctrine only in words.
E0074.body: Atwood treats the Ethnics' and Hebrew teachings as one in substance: “the assertions of the Ethnics, about the Anima Mundi, differ very little or nothing in substance from the Hebrew doctrine, but in words only” [I.2 ¶14]. The record does not define the term further.

E0075.summary: Atwood's term for the modern discovery that produces Trance and healing effects. She treats it as one name among several for an unknown agency.
E0075.body: Atwood presents Animal Magnetism as a modern discovery that produces Trance and healing effects. She treats the name as a provisional label: “Animal Magnetism, or Mesmerism, or Vital Magnetism, or by whatever other term the unknown agency is better expressed” [II.2 ¶6]. **Identities:** = Mesmerism; = Vital Magnetism [II.2 ¶6].

E0076.summary: In Eudoxus's account, the Mercury obtained once the King's bath is prepared with the blood of the Innocents. It never loses its virtue if kept well sealed.
E0076.body: Eudoxus is the speaker, quoted by Atwood. Once the King's bath has been prepared with the blood of the Innocents, “you will have the animated Mercury of the wise, which never loses its virtue” as long as it is kept in a well-closed vessel [IV.3 ¶10]. The record does not give a plain meaning for these figures.

E0077.summary: Named in the Appendix as being Venus and Lune.
E0077.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860, a later layer), Anne Bronte is said to be Venus and Lune [APP ¶175]. The record gives no further context, and it is unclear who is speaking.

E0078.summary: The state into which the artist brings all by pressing out the waters of nature's extreme life, after which nature reacts.
E0078.body: In Atwood's account, the artist presses out “the waters of her extreme life”, and nature reacts “when the wise artist has brought all into this annihilate condition” [I.2 ¶36]. Apparently this is a stage of the work in which the subject is reduced to the extreme before it revives. The text gives the sequence but no fuller definition.

E0079.summary: Atwood's term for the end of Wisdom, a so-called annihilation that leads back into the Nothing that is before all things.
E0079.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860, a later layer), Atwood places the end of Wisdom in “that so-called annihilation bringing back into the Nothing which is before all things” [APP ¶90]. Her “so-called” suggests that she is not using the word in its ordinary sense of destruction.

forms: the anonymous author of the Tractatus Aureus
E0080.summary: The unnamed author of the Tractatus Aureus, cited as having carefully prepared the magic Key that opens the door into the Hermetic garden.
E0080.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860, a later layer), this author of the *Tractatus Aureus* (Museum Hermeticum, edit. 1649, p. 45) is cited with approval as having carefully prepared the magic Key that opens the door into the Hermetic garden [APP ¶100].

E0081.summary: An unnamed authority quoted as showing the same matter to be the source of blessed waters.
E0081.body: An unnamed authority is quoted on the same matter as the source of blessed waters: “Ex mari meo oriuntur nebulae” [II.3 ¶18]. (Our translation: From my sea the mists arise.)

E0082.summary: In Aristotle's view as Atwood reports it, the cause that the human Understanding is brought into contact with through mystical exercises and preparations.
E0082.body: This is Aristotle's view as Atwood reports it. Through mystical exercises and preparations, “the human Understanding Medium is made to pass into contact with its Antecedent Cause” [II.1 ¶37]. The record does not define the term further.

E0083.summary: Atwood's term for the life that comes before outward experience and underlies it. Experience could reveal it if perception were turned inward and the obstacles removed.
E0083.body: Atwood argues that if the outward-looking faculty were turned inward and its obstacles removed, “experience might then reveal to us the antecedent life” [II.2 ¶21]. This makes the inward turning of perception a condition of the method. According to the record, the antecedent life is the life prior to and underlying outward experience.

E0085.summary: The Alchemists' Antimonial Spirit, rectified by Art and balanced between attraction and repulsion. It alone withstands life's drift toward dissolution.
E0085.body: This is the Alchemists' term, cited via Bohme. Their “Antimonial Spirit rectified by Art” [II.1 ¶20] is described as balanced between attraction and repulsion. It is the only thing that resists life's drift toward dissolution.

E0086.summary: The adepts' name for the matter of the tincture and for the fire of life. It is not the ordinary mineral, and Basil Valentine calls its preparation the key of Alchemy.
E0086.body:
Antimony appears only in quoted voices, mostly Basil Valentine's. Atwood adds a gloss of her own.

- **Not the common substance.** For the adept and Basil Valentine, Antimony names the matter of the tincture. The “oil of this antimony” is “not made of crude melted antimony, such as the apothecaries and merchants sell”, but is drawn from “the true mineral” [II.1 ¶25].
- **Fire of life.** The Paracelsians speak of “our fire of life (called Antimony by adepts” [III.1 ¶10]. **Identity:** = fire of life.
- **Key of Alchemy.** Basil Valentine says “in the preparation of Antimony consists the Key of Alchemy”. It is matured with the corporeal fire of the microcosm [III.1 ¶37]. **Identity:** = stone of Fire: “our stone of Fire (which is Antimony)” [III.1 ¶37].
- **Fixed medicine.** “Our Antimony, says Basil Valentine, which is fixed, searcheth out fixed diseases and eradicates them”, but only after all its venomous impurity has been removed [IV.1 ¶40]. Atwood explains this removal as the purging of self-will and other vices from the operator's mind. This reading is hers, and it ties the substance to the operator's own purification.

E0087.summary: Named by Atwood among the dark presences at the conjunction. The text does not define it.
E0087.body: Atwood names it among the dark presences at the conjunction: “Night, Saturn and the Antimony of the Wise will be present” [III.3 ¶13]. The record does not define it. Compare Antimony.

E0088.summary: Cited as the source of the well-known image of the Brazen Wall.
E0088.body: Atwood names Antiquity as the source of the well-known image of the Brazen Wall [IV.1 ¶4].

E0089.summary: Atwood's name for the cave-like place of descent, which she reads as the heavy, inelastic nether air bordering on the chaos of matter.
E0089.body: Atwood describes this place of descent as having air “destitute of elasticity, Aornus, heavy like that of an enclosed cave, and vast” [II.3 ¶18]. She reads it as the heavy lower air bordering on the chaos of matter. The text supports only this physical description. Any further role in the work would be inference.

E0090.summary: Invoked by Atwood to show how deeply the truth is hidden: enough to puzzle even Apollo.
E0090.body: Atwood says the truth is so wrapped up that it “might puzzle Apollo himself to explicate the whole Enigma” [IV.4 ¶2]. She uses Apollo only as a figure of speech.

E0091.summary: Quoted through Vaughan on the Brahmans, whose way of dwelling illustrates the philosophers' habitation.
E0091.body: Atwood quotes Apollonius through Vaughan: “I have seen, says Apollonius, the Brahmans of India dwelling on the earth and not on the earth” [II.4 ¶11]. She uses this as an illustration of the philosophers' habitation.

E0092.summary: Cited in footnotes, in the Argonautics and Fawkes's translation, as a parallel to the terror caused by Achilles' armour.
E0092.body: Two footnotes cite Apollonius Rhodius (Argonaut., Lib. 2; Fawkes’ Apollonius Rhodius Argonautics, Book 1) as a reference or parallel for the terror caused by Achilles' armour: “So the gloomy god/Stood mute with fearto see the golden rode” [III.1 n32, III.1 n35].

E0093.summary: The Apostle's scriptural words, which Atwood cites repeatedly to support the nearness of being, transformation, resurrection and the spiritual purification of the operator.
E0093.body:
Atwood cites the Apostle as scriptural support, always with approval:

- **Nearness of being** (Act 17:27, 28): “He is not far off from every one of us; for in Him we live, and move, and have our being” [II.1 ¶26, II.1 n24].
- **Light to light.** His “and from glory to glory” supports Agrippa's “light to light” [II.4 ¶19].
- **Resurrection** (1 Corinthians 15). This answers how what is destroyed can increase. It covers the law of resurrection, the natural body followed by the spiritual body, and leaven: “that which is sown is not the body that shall be, but mere grain” [III.3 ¶23, III.3 n13, III.3 ¶24, III.3 n17].
- **The veil lifted.** When one turns to the Lord or the Spirit, the veil over the reading of Moses is lifted, “the veil shall be taken away”, and those who behold are transformed [III.3 ¶59, III.3 n38].
- **Spiritual warfare** (2 Corinth. 10:4, 5). The purification of the operator is spiritual, not carnal: “the weapons of this warfare are not carnal, as the Apostle teaches” [IV.1 ¶40, IV.1 n33].
- **Trial by Fire** (1 Corinth. 3:11-17). The one foundation, man as the Temple of God, and “the Fire shall try every man’s work of what sort it is” are tied to Atwood's call to press on to Divine Perfection [IV.1 ¶46, IV.1 n41].

E0094.summary: Atwood's term for the final stage of the church's mysteries, which was kept most secret.
E0094.body: Atwood mentions the church's mysteries, “especially those that relate to the final apotheosis”, as the part kept most secret [II.2 ¶5]. The record does not explain it further.
